lore.creature: Jiaoren (鮫人, jiāorén), the sea people
lore.from: Chinese folklore: the South Sea, in books from the 3rd to the 6th century and in Tang poetry
lore.title: The Jiaoren
facts: Beyond the South Sea live the jiaoren. They live in the water like fish.
Jiaoren never stop weaving. They weave in the Dragon-Silk Palace deep under the South Sea, and some of their silk is as white as frost.
When a jiaoren weeps, her tears turn into pearls.
Jiaoren silk was called dragon silk. It cost more than a hundred pieces of gold.
Clothes made of jiaoren silk go into water and come out dry.
Sometimes a jiaoren came out of the sea and stayed at a person's house for a few days, selling her silk.
When she left, she asked her host for a plate, wept into it, and gave the plate back full of pearls.
The jiaoren were also called spring guests (quanke) and quanxian. A poem of the 200s calls them the guests of the deep, who are moved and weep pearls.
Old Chinese books say that pearl oysters are full when the moon is full, and empty when the moon is dark.
The poet Li Shangyin wrote of the moonlit sea, where the pearls have tears.
In Chinese medicine, pearls ground to a fine powder were used to soothe and heal.
On Mount Yuanqiao lived the ice silkworm. Covered in frost and snow, it spun a cocoon a foot long, and cloth woven from it would not get wet or burn.

In the southern mountains lived the Muke, the 'wood guests'. They traded timber without ever showing their faces, and they wrote poems. A Tang poem says the mountain people traded with the jiaoren and married the Muke.
story: Far beyond the South Sea, deeper than any fisherman has ever dived, there is a palace. Its halls are pale coral and mother-of-pearl, and in every one of them a loom is working. It never stops, not by day and not by night.

This is the Dragon-Silk Palace, the home of the jiaoren: the sea people of old Chinese books, who live in the water like fish and weave like no one on land. Their silk is so fine that the old books call it dragon silk. Some of it is as white as frost, a single length of it costs more than a hundred pieces of gold, and a robe made from it goes into the sea and comes out dry.
But the most famous thing about the jiaoren is their tears. When a jiaoren weeps, every tear turns into a pearl.

Once, the story goes, a jiaoren came up out of the sea and stayed at a person's house as a guest. For some days she sold her silk in the town. When it was time to go home, she asked her host for an empty plate. She wept into it, and handed it back full of pearls: her thank-you for the kindness.

So the jiaoren are also called the spring guests. And when poets looked at the moon shining on the sea, they thought of them. "Moonlight on the wide sea," wrote the poet Li Shangyin, "and the pearls have tears."
